title: Education Is Not Filling a Bucket but Lighting a Fire
description: Education and professional life, and the four structures the module hides inside them: the vocabulary of learning today, from the blackboard, the slate and the classroom rows to distance learning, electronic learning, CALL and CALT, the ladder that runs from a GED test through an associate, a bachelor's, a graduate certificate, a master's and a doctoral degree to non-credit training courses, and the eight advantages the book lists for a screen, from no formal class attendance to learn while you earn; special education, also called SPED or defectology, with the nine labels of the module — hearing, speech, visual and physical impairment, mental retardation, learning disabilities, emotional disturbances, chronic and long-term health problems — the difference between an impairment and a disability, mainstreaming as the practice of taking children with disabilities into regular school programmes, and the words of the case study, plight, self-esteem, impatient, switch, transfer, rely, seek and willing; modified comparatives, with the three bands of strength (a bit and a little, rather, much, far, a lot and very much), the any and the no that measure no step at all, and the many more of a countable noun against the much more and much less of an uncountable one; comparison of scale, the structure of the module — multiplier plus as plus adjective or adverb plus as, and multiplier plus as plus many or much plus an optional noun plus as — with twice, three times, half, a third and a quarter, the base adjective inside the block and the reading of a scale backwards; status against pay, with white-collar and blue-collar workers, the dustman, the clerk, the overalls and the rise in status of Alfred Bloggs; the stages of a job search, from the employment agency and the application form to the qualifications, the interview, the wages and the promotion, and the recorded interview of a product manager; indirect questions, introduced by ask, inquire, wonder and want to know, with the WH word that is kept, the if or whether of a yes/no question, the statement word order that drops do, does and did, and the backshift of tenses after a past reporting verb; the main stress of a word ending in -tion or -sion, and the sounds behind th, ch, ough and i; school discipline, with disruptive, unruly, disobedient, muck around, praise, heap, youngsters, prior, shift, quarrel, prestigious and ridiculous, the four punishments ranged from lines and detention to suspension and exclusion, and the argumentative newspaper article that defends praising unruly pupils and prints the objections to it; relative pronouns and the two kinds of relative clause, restrictive without commas and able to drop an object pronoun, non-restrictive between commas and never taking that; the phrases of disapproval, reproach, warning, concession, apology and intention used at a meeting about a poor school report, with extra-curricular, involved, sit for an exam, strength and weakness; and the report on a book, with its three-part plan and the division of work between the simple present of the plot and the simple past of the reading
